question: Why do people pray witr in different ways, and which way should I follow?
asked: I come from a particular background, and since coming to this country I have seen people pray witr in different manners, in taraweeh and in other situations. I'm now confused. What is to be done in this regard?
answer:
The response, my dear brother in Islam, is that the witr is one of those prayers in which pretty much all of the madhahib have slightly different answers. And so whichever madhhab you were upon, you may choose that madhhab and follow it, no problem. It is a very, very trivial matter which of the positions you follow, inshaAllah. They're all telling you to pray witr, and they're all wanting you to do the prayer. The differences are in the minor details, or the minutiae, if you like.

And the witr prayer is of course called witr because the term witr means odd. The witr prayer is an odd prayer; it's always an odd number of raka'at. So three raka'at is the default position of most of the madhhabs, and the Hanafi madhhab specifies three in particular. And it's an odd number.

And our Prophet ﷺ strongly commanded the people, or strongly suggested, depending on how you would interpret it, to pray witr. In the famous hadith in Bukhari and Muslim, Abu Hurairah (radiyAllahu 'anhu) said that my friend, meaning the Prophet ﷺ, commanded me with three things. Wassa means to put it very strongly. Three things: number one, to fast three days of every month; number two, to pray two raka'at of Salat al-Duha, which is basically from an hour after Fajr until Salat al-Dhuhr; and number three, to pray witr before I go to sleep: wa an utira qabla an anam.

So the Prophet wanted Abu Hurairah to reach a high level, and he's putting on Abu Hurairah certain extra things that he should do: fasting three days of every month; praying Salat al-Duha, also called the Ishraq prayer, which is, as we said, the early sunnah prayer after the sun rises until Salat al-Dhuhr; and then number three, to pray witr before I go to sleep, meaning that in case you are not waking up for tahajjud, you pray witr before you go to sleep.

And it is reported in Abu Dawud that Ali said that the Prophet ﷺ said, "O people of the Qur'an, pray witr, because Allah 'azza wa jall Himself is witr," meaning one, "and He loves the witr," meaning the witr prayer. And He loves witr. So this hadith says, "O people of the Qur'an." Some have said that "O people of the Qur'an" means "O Muslims," because we all believe in the Qur'an. And others have said that the Prophet ﷺ is especially saying to those who have memorized the Qur'an in particular that they should not spend the whole night asleep. They should pray a witr prayer and pray some extra prayers above and beyond the five prayers.

And in another hadith, reported in Musnad Ahmad, 'Amr ibn al-'As (radiyAllahu 'anhu) gave a khutbah on the day of Jumu'ah, in public. And he said that the Prophet ﷺ told us (so he's giving the khutbah, and in the khutbah he's telling all of the people there what he heard from the Prophet ﷺ) that Allah has added a prayer for all of you to pray, and it is the prayer of witr, so pray the witr between Salat al-Isha and Salat al-Fajr. This hadith is reported in Musnad Imam Ahmad: Allah has added a prayer for you, so pray it between Isha and Fajr.

Now, these ahadith all mention some of the blessings of witr, and there are other ahadith as well. And based on these ahadith, and also based upon the Hanafi school's categorization of actions... Pause here, footnote. I mentioned in another Q&A many, many months ago, I think almost a year and a half ago, that the Hanafis have seven categorizations of all actions, and the other madhahib have five categorizations. So the Hanafis take the fard and the wajib and make them two different things. And they take makruh and say makruh tanzihi and makruh tahrimi. And so what they have basically is two categories of obligatory and two categories of sin, whereas the rest of the schools have one category of obligatory and one category of sin. So they say fard and wajib are the same, whereas for the Hanafis, fard is higher than wajib. And the same goes for the other side of the spectrum.

So the Hanafis say the five salawat are fard and the witr is wajib, meaning if you do not pray witr, you are sinful in the eyes of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala, because they have that category: wajib is something that is obligatory to do, but, let's just be simplistic, not to the level of the fard. The other three schools don't have that distinction; they simply have strongly encouraged and obligatory. And based on this categorization, witr cannot come under obligatory. And so the other three schools basically have it at the very, very highest level of strongly encouraged. In other words, right underneath obligatory, they would have Salat al-Witr. So if you don't pray witr, according to the other three schools, Allah is not going to punish you in Jahannam for not praying witr, but you're really falling short. And it's the most important of all of the sunan prayers, all of the non-wajib prayers; the three madhhabs say it is at the strongest level.

So this is in terms of its nature: is it obligatory or is it not? And each of the schools has its evidences. And at the end of the day, I think as Imam Ahmad said, how can a Muslim not pray witr? He considered the one who doesn't pray witr as somebody whose testimony should not be accepted in a court of law, for example. According to his paradigm, how can he be trusted if he's going to be so lazy as to not even pray witr at the end of the night?

And so let's not really get involved in whether it's obligatory or not. Let's just try to pray witr, because it is definitely something that the Prophet ﷺ strongly, strongly, strongly encouraged us to pray. And in his own actions ﷺ, he never ever stopped praying witr. Even when he was traveling, he would pray witr. When he was traveling, he would not pray the other regular sunan of Dhuhr and Maghrib and after Isha, but he would pray witr, and he would pray the two raka'at before Fajr. These are the two that he would pray when he was traveling. So let us make sure that we pray our witr.

Now, that's the first issue. The second issue: what is the timing of witr? Here we have basically no controversy at all amongst the scholars that the timing of witr is any time after you pray Salat al-Isha until the crack before the time of Fajr, basically, until the dawn breaks. Not the sunrise, but the dawn breaking, i.e. that line that comes and signifies the time of Fajr. So witr is from after Isha, whenever you pray Isha, until the timing of Fajr; it can be prayed at any time.

And our Prophet ﷺ said in a famous hadith in Sahih Muslim and others that whoever is worried that he's not going to pray witr at the end of the night, then let him pray witr in the beginning of the night. And whoever thinks that he can pray at the end, let him pray at the end of the night, because the prayer at the end of the night is going to be witnessed by the angels, and that is more blessed. So this hadith tells us that the ideal timing for witr is pre-Fajr.

And this leads us to our next point, and that is that the concept of witr is linked to, but not necessarily attached to, the concept of tahajjud. So witr could imply all of tahajjud, and you can call all of tahajjud witr, because at the end of the day you will pray an odd number of raka'at. So you will pray eight plus three; that is eleven, that's like all of your tahajjud. Therefore, sometimes when the term witr is used in the hadith, it implies all of the tahajjud and the three raka'at at the end, and sometimes it only applies to that very last three raka'at.

And so, for example, in the hadith of Abu Hurairah, in which he said that my friend advised me to pray witr before I go to sleep, what he means here is Salat al-Tahajjud. Let's give an example: suppose that Isha is at 8:30 PM and you go to sleep at 11 PM, and for whatever reason you don't wake up for tahajjud; you wake up for Salat al-Fajr. So what Abu Hurairah is saying is that I will pray Isha at 8:30, then whatever needs to be done, then before 11 o'clock, before going to sleep, I will pray the whole tahajjud and then go to sleep. So Abu Hurairah, because he was busy with hadith, because for a period of his life he was very engrossed in memorizing and whatnot, would pray tahajjud before going to sleep. And that is a permissible time for tahajjud. And he called witr tahajjud.

Now, most of us, when we use the term witr, what we mean by it is the specific three raka'at only. And that's fine; nothing wrong with that terminology. When most of us use the term witr, that is what we mean.

Now the Hanafis, as we said, said that the three-raka'at witr prayer is going to be just like Salat al-Maghrib: you will pray three raka'at, you will sit down in the second raka'ah, you will say the tashahhud, and then you will stand up, and then you will sit down in the third raka'ah, and you will then have one taslim at the end. So for the Hanafi madhhab, Maghrib and witr resemble one another.

As well, the Hanafis are the strictest out of all of the schools when it comes to qunut. A lot of the Hanafi brethren are not aware of this: the other three madhahib do not have the qunut as such a necessary part of witr. Some of them say it is allowed or mustahabb, but in practice, as we're going to come to, basically none of the other madhhabs (i.e. the followers of those madhahib, generally speaking) do qunut in witr. But the Hanafis, as all of us from a Hanafi background are aware, associate witr with qunut. And for the other schools, qunut is a separate du'a, and it is not necessarily linked with witr to the level of the Hanafis.

The Hanbalis and the Shafi'is allow the qunut in the witr. As I said, the Shafi'is and the Hanbalis allow it, and in fact the Hanbalis say it is even encouraged, but they do not make it something that is basically an integral part. And in practice, most of the followers of the Shafi'i school and most of the followers of the Hanbali school do not do it, because the madhhab is not that strict upon it. It is something allowed; if you want to do it, go ahead and do it.

And the Hanafi school is the strictest when it comes to the du'a of the witr. There's a special du'a, they call it Du'a al-Qunut, as we know, and it is done before the last ruku'. There are also reports within the Hanbali madhhab that the witr should only have the qunut in the very last days of Ramadan. And this is a report also from the Maliki madhhab: that the qunut, the du'a, should be associated with the witr only in the month of Ramadan, and some even add in the last half of Ramadan, like the last ten nights of Ramadan. So these are all positions about the qunut vis-à-vis the witr; all of them are narrated and permissible.

As well, there is quite a lot of difference of opinion about the procedure of praying witr. I said that the Hanafis pray three raka'at continuously with one taslim. The Maliki school said that it is better to pray two raka'at, then make a taslim, then stand up and pray one raka'ah on its own. So the Maliki school breaks the three raka'at into two halves. And they base this on a hadith of Aisha (radiyAllahu 'anha), that she said that the Prophet would pray witr when in my room, in my hujrah, in my chambers or compartment, and I was in the house at that time, and he would separate between the two raka'at and the witr, and I would hear the taslim between the two of them. So they use that narration.

And the other evidence that they have is a hadith reported in al-Daraqutni and the Mustadrak of al-Hakim, that our Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said, "Do not perform the witr with three raka'at, or else it will look like Salat al-Maghrib." So this hadith has been interpreted by the other schools, and especially the Maliki school, to say that the two raka'at should be separated with the taslim, and then you stand up and pray one raka'ah. The Maliki school did not associate qunut with witr. For them, witr is simply the odd number. And they also allowed, even though they didn't encourage, one raka'ah: if you don't want to pray the two raka'at and just pray one raka'ah, it will still be witr.

The Shafi'i school said that three raka'at is the minimum of perfection, and you can pray more. So the Shafi'is said witr is five and seven and nine, no problem. And they said, yes, if you really want to, we'll allow you to pray one, but that's like makruh; you really shouldn't pray only one. Three is the minimum of perfection, and it's even better to pray more than that, because again, for them, the concepts of witr and tahajjud are kind of combined. And so when you're praying witr, it is kind of sort of a tahajjud; you might as well make it five or seven or nine.

And the Shafi'is said that you pray all three raka'at continuously, without sitting down in the second raka'ah. This is the preferred position. And some said you pray two raka'at, then you do the taslim, and then you do one raka'ah. So the Shafi'i madhhab did not want to resemble the Maghrib prayer, based on the hadith that they have, and so they wanted to go a different route. And they said you either pray three continuously without sitting down in the second: number one, number two, you get back up, and then number three, then you make the taslim.

And of course, both the Shafi'is and the Hanbalis also said that it is preferred to recite Surat al-A'la in the first raka'ah, and then Surat al-Kafirun in the second raka'ah, and then Ikhlas and Falaq and Nas in the third raka'ah. Also, the Shafi'is were the madhhab that said qunut should only be done in the last part of Ramadan during witr, and not throughout the year. In fact, the Shafi'i school has Du'a al-Qunut in Fajr salah, by the way, and that's why all of the Arab brothers from Jordan and from Egypt and whatnot are aware that the Shafi'i school prays qunut in Fajr. And in the Hanafi school, in India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, the qunut is done in witr. And in the Hanbali school, in theory it is also in witr, it is encouraged, but in practice they really don't do qunut except at times of calamities, when they will do that. So this is the Shafi'i school.

The Hanbali school said that it should also be done in three, and to do less than three is allowed, but it is not something that should be encouraged. You can pray one, but it is makruh, yet it is also accepted. And they also encouraged praying two plus one, and they also allowed the Hanafi way of doing it as well. So the Hanbali madhhab, as usual, has plenty of positions about this. And they said that qunut is encouraged, but as I said, in practice they did not actually do the du'a al-qunut. Also, by the way, for most of the Hanbalis the qunut is done after the ruku', whereas for the Hanafis the qunut is done before the ruku'.

All of this was a quick kaleidoscope to explain to you that all of these positions have been narrated. At the end of the day, dear brother in Islam, don't worry about the other schools. You have heard your particular school (most likely, I'm assuming, you're from a Hanafi background); no problem, then you pray the Hanafi procedure. These are very trivial issues: whether you pray two and then taslim and then one, or you pray three; whether you do the qunut before the ruku', after the ruku', or you don't do it at all if you're Maliki or Shafi'i. No problem; whatever is done, these are all trivial things. **The main point is that we pray Salat al-Witr**, and that, inshaAllah ta'ala, we strive to follow the Sunnah of the Prophet in this regard, because we know that witr is one of the most encouraged of all of the sunnah prayers.
